title: Receiving Feedback & Disagreement
summary: Responding to review comments professionally, including the harder case of disagreeing with them — when to push back, when to disagree-and-commit, and how to escalate without burning trust.

slides.markdown:
Giving good feedback is only half the exchange. The other half — receiving it, especially when you disagree — is where a lot of engineers who are otherwise strong reviewers struggle, because it's the moment where ego and correctness are hardest to separate.

The default posture that keeps a review productive: assume good intent, and respond to the substance of the comment rather than how it made you feel. When you genuinely disagree, the skill is arguing with evidence rather than just asserting you're right, and knowing how to move forward once a decision is actually made — even one you didn't want.

This topic is about the author's side of the exchange: how to take a comment well, how to disagree well, and what to do when disagreement doesn't resolve on its own.

Text strips out tone. A terse comment — "this won't scale" — can read as an attack when it was written in thirty seconds between meetings with zero ill intent behind it. The default assumption that keeps review functional: the reviewer is trying to make the code better, not trying to make you look bad.

This matters practically because the alternative default — assuming hostility until proven otherwise — makes every terse comment a small crisis, and authors who operate that way burn energy on imagined slights instead of the actual technical question. It also changes how you *read* the comment: "this won't scale" parsed charitably is a request for the scaling argument, not a verdict.

This doesn't mean tolerating comments that are actually hostile — it means not manufacturing hostility out of brevity, which is the far more common case.

Two different reactions get bundled together and shouldn't be: **"I disagree with this specific suggestion"** and **"I feel criticized."** The first is a technical position you can argue for. The second is an emotional reaction that, left unexamined, often gets expressed *as if* it were the first — a defensive rebuttal to a comment that wasn't actually wrong, just uncomfortable to receive.

The tell: if your response to a comment is about the comment's *tone* rather than its *content*, you're probably reacting to feeling criticized, not disagreeing with the suggestion. Worth naming that to yourself before replying — a comment that stings can still be correct, and a reply that argues with the tone instead of the substance doesn't move the PR forward.

Separating the two isn't about suppressing the emotional reaction. It's about not letting it masquerade as a technical argument it isn't.

Disagreeing with a review comment is not a violation of process — it's often the correct response, and a reviewer who's never been pushed back on is either always right or working with authors who never challenge them, and the second is worse.

The difference between productive pushback and stonewalling is **evidence**. "I don't think that's right" is an assertion. "I don't think that's right — this path only runs during startup, before any concurrent requests exist, so the lock you're asking for adds overhead with no correctness benefit" is an argument the reviewer can actually evaluate and potentially concede to.

Bring the same rigor to disagreeing that you'd want the original comment held to: a specific mechanism, not a vibe. If you can't articulate the mechanism, that's often a sign the reviewer's concern is more valid than your discomfort with it suggests.

Sometimes the reviewer and author lay out their full arguments and still don't converge, and someone has to make the call — the reviewer as the approver, a tech lead, or whoever owns that part of the system. **Disagree and commit** is the practice of executing the decision fully once it's made, even though you argued the other way.

The failure mode this prevents is worse than losing the argument: an author who implements the agreed approach half-heartedly, or keeps re-litigating it in later PRs, creates a slower and more contentious version of the same outcome they were trying to avoid. If you commit, commit — sloppy compliance to "prove it was wrong" is a form of sabotage, even when unintentional.

The flip side matters equally: disagree-and-commit only works if raising the disagreement in the first place was genuinely safe. A team that punishes pushback trains people to stop bringing up real concerns, which is a much larger cost than losing one argument.

Not every disagreement resolves between the two people in the thread, and that's fine — it's what an escalation path is for. Bringing in a third opinion isn't a failure of the review process, it's a designed part of it.

A workable path looks like: state both positions neutrally in one place (not "they're wrong," but "here's the tradeoff we see differently"), tag a tech lead or a relevant domain owner, and ask for a decision rather than a vote — someone needs to actually own the call, not just add a third opinion to a pile of two.

What makes escalation work well is framing it as seeking clarity, not as recruiting an ally against the other person. "Can you help us decide between X and Y" lands very differently from "can you tell them they're wrong," even when the underlying facts are identical — the first invites a decision, the second invites a side to be picked.

slides.sectionTitle: Comment thread vs a quick call
slides.markdown:
Disagreement can resolve two ways, and picking the wrong one wastes real time:

| | Async back-and-forth | Quick call |
|---|---|---|
| **Best for** | clear-cut technical points, decisions needing a written record | genuine misunderstanding, nuance that's hard to convey in text |
| **Speed** | can take hours across timezones for a few exchanges | resolves in minutes if both are available |
| **Record** | automatically documented in the PR | needs a follow-up comment to capture the outcome |
| **Failure mode** | a three-day, ten-comment thread over something a five-minute call would settle | a decision made verbally and never written down, re-litigated later |

A rough signal for switching to a call: if you're on your third round of the same point without either side updating their position, text isn't the bottleneck — tone and nuance are getting lost, and a call resolves in minutes what the thread hasn't in a day. Whoever calls it should still post a one-line summary back on the PR so the resolution isn't lost to a call nobody else was on.

slides.subTitle: The disagreement nobody hears
slides.markdown:
The failure mode that's worse than an argued disagreement is the one that never surfaces: an author who thinks a comment is wrong, implements it anyway without saying so, and quietly resents both the comment and the reviewer. Nothing about this is visible in the PR — it looks like a clean, agreeable merge.

The cost shows up later and sideways: the same disagreement resurfaces in the next PR, still unresolved, now with accumulated frustration attached. Or the author starts routing around that reviewer entirely, requesting review from someone less likely to push back — which quietly degrades the whole team's review quality.

The fix isn't complicated, just uncomfortable: say the disagreement out loud, in the thread, even briefly — "I don't think this is necessary, but I'll make the change; happy to talk through it if useful." That single sentence turns invisible resentment into a visible, resolvable data point.

```text
Reviewer: blocking: this should use a database transaction —
otherwise a crash between these two writes leaves the record
half-updated.

Author: I don't think a transaction is needed here — both writes
go to the same row via a single UPDATE with two SET clauses, so
they're already atomic at the database level. Wrapping a single
statement in a transaction wouldn't add anything. Am I missing a
case where they'd actually be separate writes?

Reviewer: Good point, I misread it as two separate UPDATE calls.
Single statement is fine as is.
```

The author didn't just say "I disagree" — they gave the specific mechanism (single UPDATE, already atomic) that let the reviewer check their own claim and concede. Compare that to "I don't think that's needed," which would have forced a second round of back-and-forth to even locate the actual disagreement.

Junior engineers often treat every review comment as either "comply" or "argue to win." The senior version has a third mode: recognizing that some disagreements aren't worth the cost of resolving fully, and knowing which ones those are.

If a comment suggests a marginally different approach with no meaningful difference in correctness, maintainability, or performance, the efficient move is to just make the change and move on — not because the reviewer is right, but because the cost of arguing exceeds the cost of complying. Save the pushback and the escalation energy for disagreements where the outcome actually matters.

This is a judgment call that improves with experience: knowing which hill is worth taking is as much a skill as the arguing itself, and confusing "I have an opinion" with "this is worth a three-comment thread" is a common junior mistake.

Receiving feedback well is: assume good intent by default, separate genuine disagreement from feeling criticized, argue with mechanism and evidence when you do disagree, commit fully once a decision is made, escalate to a third opinion rather than let a stalemate rot, and say disagreement out loud instead of swallowing it.

How the review process itself is structured — PR size, ownership, SLAs, and how much of this friction gets automated away — is the next topic in this group.
